newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians mourn victims of grenade attack.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians mourn victims of grenade attack.

text.p: Cambodians on Monday mourned the victims of a weekend grenade attack on an opposition protest that killed at least 14 people, and the Interior Ministry said it was still unclear who was responsible.

The attack outside the National Assembly in Phnom Penh was the worst and most blatant act of political violence to hit Cambodia's fragile democracy since the current coalition government came to power after United Nations-organised elections in May 1993.

Protest leader and apparent target Sam Rainsy, who narrowly escaped injury, has blamed the attack on his bitter foe, co- premier Hun Sen. But an Interior Ministry spokesman said it was unclear who was responsible and an investigation was underway.

"Until now, police have found no clues as to who was responsible," Interior Ministry spokesman Sok Phal said. "The Ministry of Interior has started a thorough investigation to discover the perpetrators and those behind them."
Aides to Hun Sen and co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said the two had set up a joint investigation committee.

A witness said four grenades were thrown from a car that sped past the protest, but Rainsy said at least one was thrown from inside the assembly compound, in the heart of the capital just metres (yards) from the royal palace.
There were conflicting reports as to the number killed.
Doctors at the three major Phnom Penh hospitals that took in casualties said nine people had died in hospital or arrived there dead. Police said on Sunday that seven died at the scene.
The chairman of parliament, Loy Sim Chheang, issued a statement condemning the attack on what he said was a legal protest and put the death toll at 14 with more than 100 injured.

Sam Rainsy told Reuters on Monday afternoon that up to 20 people had died, and a spokesman for Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party that rules in an uneasy coalition with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) also put the toll at up to 20.

Loy Sim Chheang's statement said the government must bring those responsible to justice. "This recent crime shows that our Kingdom of Cambodia still uses violence against innocent people which is increasing in its brutality," it said.
Mak Chito, head of the Phnom Penh police's serious crimes office, called the attack "a big tragedy in Cambodian history", but added: "There is still no evidence."
On Sunday, Hun Sen blamed the attack on terrorists, but he also said those responsible for the demonstration should be arrested.
Asked if Sam Rainsy would be arrested, Mak Chito said this would depend on the findings of the investigation.
On Monday, mourners lay flowers and burnt incense on the pavement outside the assembly, still stained with blood and littered with the footwear and clothing of some of the victims.
Sam Rainsy's wife Tioulong Saumura told Reuters it was only the latest attempt on her husband's life.
"He has been constantly under threat," she said.
Sunday's protest was against what Sam Rainsy termed the domination of the judiciary by the CPP.
On Monday, he said the CPP was "more and more deliberately and malignantly violating the law and the constitution...there is no democracy here. Any dissident can eliminated at any time."

Sam Rainsy became Hun Sen's strongest critic after being fired as finance minister in 1994. He was expelled from parliament in 1995 and his Khmer Nation Party is not recognised by the government, though it recently formed an alliance with Ranariddh's royalists.
The opposition leader said First Prime Minister Ranariddh had promised him that he would try and use his influence with Hun Sen to calm the situation.
